analysis.one_liner: Cancels federal student loans up to Pell Grant totals and raises the maximum Pell Grant.
analysis.headline: Introduced in June 2022 with zero cosponsors, the bill was referred to the Senate Finance Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would cancel federal student loans for borrowers who ever received a Pell Grant — the aid program for lower-income students — up to the total amount of Pell money they received, across Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans. It would raise the maximum Pell Grant from about $7,000 to $9,000 in 2024-25 and step it up to $13,000 by 2032-33. It would also end interest capitalization and origination fees on new Direct Loans, collapse repayment into two simple plans — a fixed 10-year plan and an income-based plan with $0 payments for people under 250% of the poverty line and forgiveness after 20 years — and limit how much collectors can garnish from wages or benefits.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers who received Pell Grants would have a large share of their federal loans cancelled — up to every Pell dollar they received. Future low-income students would get bigger grants that don't have to be repaid. All borrowers would benefit from lower loan balances over time once interest capitalization and origination fees ended, delinquent borrowers would be automatically moved into affordable income-based payments, and collectors could no longer seize more from wages or benefits than the income-based plan would require.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Pell Grant recipients with federal loans

how_it_helps.text: Cancels principal and interest on Direct, FFEL, and Perkins loans in repayment for anyone who received a Pell Grant, up to the total amount of Pell Grants they received, within 180 days of enactment.
Raises the maximum Pell Grant to $9,000 for 2024-25 and steps it up each year to $13,000 by 2032-33, increasing money for low-income students that does not have to be repaid.

Ends interest capitalization (unpaid interest being added to principal so interest is charged on interest) and repeals origination fees on Federal Direct Loans, with the fee repeal applying to loans first disbursed on or after January 1, 2026.

Replaces the maze of repayment plans with two choices: a fixed 10-year plan and an income-based plan that charges 0% of income for borrowers at or below 250% of the poverty line, forgives remaining balances after 20 years, and uses automatic income recertification from IRS data so borrowers don't have to re-document income every year.

Limits collectors to garnishing no more than what the income-based plan would require, imposes civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per day on entities that knowingly over-seize, lets borrowers rehabilitate defaulted loans more than once, creates a single streamlined 'pause payment' process, automatically enrolls long-delinquent borrowers into income-based repayment, and allows joint spousal consolidation loans to be split — with a separate application path for survivors of domestic violence.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers bear the cost of the loan cancellations and the larger Pell Grants. Student loan servicers and debt collection companies lose revenue from ending collection costs, limiting garnishment, and streamlining repayment, and they face new daily penalties for over-seizing income.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers; loan servicers and collectors

drawbacks.text: Loan cancellation and a Pell Grant maximum rising to $13,000 are large federal expenses, and the bill provides no offsetting revenue.
Because Pell eligibility historically reaches into middle-income households, some cancellation would go to borrowers who are now able to repay their loans.
The bill does nothing about the cost of college itself, and a larger Pell Grant could be absorbed by tuition increases rather than lowering what students pay.

Simplifying to two repayment plans eliminates graduated and extended options, and for higher earners (above 1,300% of the poverty line) the new income-based plan takes 10% of adjusted gross income with payments that may exceed the standard 10-year amount.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The relief is well targeted at people who were poor enough to qualify for Pell Grants, and the repayment and garnishment fixes address real problems — balance ballooning, surprise fees, and aggressive collection. The main honest objection is cost to the Treasury and the risk that colleges capture the bigger grants through higher tuition. The design flaws are modest relative to the direct relief for lower-income borrowers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Senator Catherine Cortez Masto introduced the bill on June 23, 2022.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day — its only action.
The bill had no cosponsors in either party.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred, and the Congress ended January 3, 2023 without further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Borrowers gained nothing because the bill never moved. Federal loan servicers and collection companies kept the repayment and collection system as it was — with origination fees, interest capitalization, collection costs, and broad garnishment powers intact — and the Treasury avoided the cost of the cancellations and larger grants.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Loan servicers, collectors, and the Treasury

against.what_they_did: Held the bill without a hearing, markup, or vote for the six months remaining in the 117th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever took place, and the bill drew zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan breakdown exists beyond its single Democratic sponsor.

industries.industry: Federal student loan servicers and debt collection agencies
industries.note: The bill would cap garnishment of wages and benefits at the income-based payment amount, eliminate the requirement that defaulted borrowers pay collection costs, and expose entities that knowingly over-seize income to civil penalties up to $1,000,000 per day. Its death left these collection powers and revenue streams intact.

The bill would strip lenders' ability to set their own repayment schedules, replacing them with two standardized plans, though forgiveness would be paid through loan holders. It never moved, so lenders' existing arrangements continued unchanged.

A Pell maximum rising to $13,000 would channel substantially more federal aid to their students — and to their revenue. Critics note that institutions rather than students can capture grant increases through higher tuition, a risk the bill does not address.
